claims.text: An integrated platform combining fast scanning calorimetry, high-temperature dilatometry, in-situ neutron imaging, and CALPHAD can determine melting temperature, fusion enthalpy and entropy, melting volume change, and liquid-phase thermodynamic properties across high-entropy alloys.
The platform can measure melting temperature with precision better than ±1%.
The platform can measure fusion enthalpy and entropy within ±5% error.
As-cast Al0.5CoCrFeNi is a representative homogeneous, single-phase HEA suitable for the platform.
Equiatomic CoCrCu(Ni) alloys are representative homogeneous, single-phase HEAs in their as-cast state.
Experiments can use rapid temperature ramps from 10 to 10^3 K/s under inert atmosphere or high vacuum.
Heating and cooling measurements can validate that equilibrium states have been reached.
Fast scanning calorimetry detects distinct endothermic peaks corresponding to melting onset in HEAs.
High-temperature dilatometry records rapid volume expansion associated with fusion in HEAs.
In-situ neutron imaging can visualize the onset and progression of melting in CoCrCu-based alloys.
In-situ neutron imaging can distinguish liquid-phase separation from remixing into a single-phase liquid in the CoCrCu-Ni system.
Neutron imaging requires sufficient differences in neutron transmission among alloying elements to provide phase contrast.
CALPHAD modeling can provide phase-equilibrium, solvus, and equilibrium-solidus information for HEAs.
Cross-referencing calorimetry, dilatometry, and neutron-imaging outputs with CALPHAD permits self-consistent extraction of all specified fusion and liquid thermodynamic properties.
A rigorously maintained calibration is necessary because furnace and sample temperatures can differ during melting measurements.
Individual FSC or dilatometry methods have larger uncertainties and inefficiencies because of kinetic and metastability limitations in HEAs.
The platform will generate a reliable, broadly applicable liquid-thermodynamics database spanning FCC, BCC, and HCP HEA families.
Applicability is limited to alloys forming single-phase liquids, as confirmed by neutron imaging and CALPHAD consistency.
Systematic temperature discrepancies greater than ±15 °C or fusion enthalpy or entropy deviations greater than ±5% against benchmarks or CALPHAD predictions would render the approach inadequate.
